title: Chinnery family suing police over shooting
subtitle: The family of a 19-year-old Hamilton man fatally shot by police two years ago has launched a $650,000 lawsuit against police.
article: The family of a 19-year-old Hamilton man fatally shot by police two years ago has launched a $650,000 lawsuit against police.

Andreas Chinnery died Feb. 2, 2011 after an altercation with police inside his Barton Street East apartment. His family is asking for compensation for the loss of Chinnery, expenses as a result of his death and other unspecified economic loss.

The lawsuit names Chinnery's father, Robert Chinnery, and siblings Sacha, Stefan and Michaela Chinnery as plaintiffs. The Hamilton Police Services Board, police Chief Glenn De Caire, an unnamed dispatcher and constables Michael McNaughton and Bryan Spencer are named as defendants.
In the statement of claim, the family argues that deadly force was negligently used, instead of considering a number of other options including calling COAST (Crisis Outreach and Support Team).
The document says McNaughton was the officer who fired the fatal shots.
None of the claims has been proven in court.
"The action of the defendants McNaughton and Spencer showed that they were contemptuous of the rights of the deceased and more concerned with their own physical well-being," the statement reads.

The family's lawyer, Graydon Sheppard, said the lawsuit is not just about compensation for the Chinnerys. Rather, he argued that they hope the "financial sting" of a lawsuit will encourage police to change their use of force practices and prevent another disturbed person from being hurt or killed.
"Other agencies don't seem to have any influence on the Hamilton Police Services," Sheppard said.
The lawsuit does not affect an inquest into Chinnery's death that began last year and is set to resume sometime later this year.
Hamilton police spokesperson Catherine Martin declined to comment on both the inquest and lawsuit "out of respect for the legal process."
Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, previously cleared the officer involved in the incident.
According to the SIU, police went to Chinnery's home after a neighbour complained he was damaging his apartment, yelling and making threats.
When officers arrived, Chinnery answered the door holding a baseball bat and hit the door jamb, the SIU said. The two officers pulled out their guns and ordered him to drop the bat.
The SIU concluded that Chinnery then yelled, stepped toward the officers and started to swing at one of them, who responded by shooting.
The Chinnery family has continually questioned the police version of events, including whether he had a bat.
In the statement of claim, they argue that another tenant at 766 Barton St. E. called police on a non-emergency line that night, reporting noise from an upstairs unit.

The plaintiffs argue that the unnamed dispatcher directed the officers to the apartment, but said the incident "involved a couple with ongoing issues and that the male was screaming at the female and threatening her with death."
When the officers arrived, they were let into the building and "seconds later" Chinnery was shot. He fell to the floor, was handcuffed and quickly bled out, reads the statement of claim.

"At no time did the defendants or those for whom they are responsible, have reasonable or probable grounds to believe that the deceased was engaged in either criminal or dangerous behaviour before he was shot."

Supporters of the Chinnery family are holding a rally and protest to mark the second anniversary of Andreas Chinnery's death Saturday. It will begin at 2 p.m. at City Hall and then progress to Hamilton police headquarters on King William Street.
